2. The bowling ball is rigid and dissipates almost all impact energy
3. Air resistance differences between them are negligible compared to this fundamental elasticity difference

# Solving the Birthday Problem (Inverse)

This question asks for the probability that **at least two people do NOT share a birthday** — meaning at least two people have *different* birthdays.

## Key Insight

The only way this *fails* (i.e., no two people have different birthdays) is if **all 30 people share the exact same birthday**.

So I need:
$$P(\text{at least two have different birthdays}) = 1 - P(\text{all 30 people have the same birthday})$$

## Calculating P(all same birthday)

For all 30 people to share the same birthday:
- Person 1 can have any birthday (365 choices)
- Person 2 must match Person 1: probability 1/365
- Person 3 must match: probability 1/365
- ... and so on for all remaining 29 people

$$P(\text{all same}) = \left(\frac{1}{365}\right)^{29}$$

This is an extraordinarily small number — astronomically close to zero.

## Final Answer

$$P(\text{at least two different birthdays}) = 1 - \left(\frac{1}{365}\right)^{29} \approx 1 - (2.6 \times 10^{-74})$$

$$\boxed{P \approx 0.999999999\ldots \approx 1}$$

**In essence: this probability is virtually certain (100%).** With 30 people, it would take an almost impossible coincidence for every single person to have the same birthday — far more unlikely than the classic birthday problem (which asks about *shared* birthdays, where the answer is a surprising ~70%).
